tldr: A real-time glass plane mapping framework that combines depth-free projective geometry verification with global hypothesis management to detect transparent glass for collision avoidance without creating false obstacles that block traversable free space.
hero_caption: Overview of the GlassGuard system. Through a three-stage pipeline—2D glass segmentation using Slim SAM3 with 3D candidate generation from LiDAR pillar features (left), depth-free orientation verification and multi-view checks using image edges (middle), and global map consolidation with floor-conflict pruning (right)—only accurate glass planes are retained in the map.
overview:
While LiDAR is widely used in autonomous mobile robots, it suffers from a critical blind spot: laser beams penetrate or specularly reflect off transparent glass, leaving obstacles undetected. Missing these surfaces can lead to direct collisions. Conversely, prior methods that attempt to reconstruct glass from visual inputs often suffer from "free-space contamination"—placing phantom walls across traversable paths due to weak texture on glass surfaces or distracting surrounding edge features.

To solve this, the authors propose "GlassGuard," a framework designed to simultaneously satisfy two core requirements: reliably closing off glass surfaces while never blocking traversable free space. Rather than delegating challenging 3D estimation end-to-end to deep learning, it divides the labor cleanly: deep learning handles 2D glass region detection, while 3D plane hypotheses are generated from surrounding LiDAR geometry. Its key novelty is a geometric verification mechanism that derives 3D orientations (yaw angles) directly from the planes swept by glass frame lines in the image—completely without depth—instantly filtering out misaligned LiDAR proposals.

In real-robot experiments across nine building-scale scenes (indoors, outdoors, day, and night) covering over 2.1 km of traversal, GlassGuard achieved 85% total glass coverage with a panoramic camera and 82% under identical pinhole camera conditions, outperforming evaluated baselines (at most 61%). Crucially, it reduced false obstacle voxels that block corridors by 5 to 17 times compared to prior approaches.
contributions: Formulated a navigation-oriented problem definition that simultaneously maximizes glass detection coverage and minimizes false occupancy (spill) in traversable free space.

Developed a depth-free monocular geometric verification mechanism that recovers physical normal directions from glass frame lines in images to screen out angular errors in LiDAR-derived candidate planes.

Constructed a global hypothesis management system that avoids prematurely finalizing planes, instead consolidating them via accumulated LiDAR seeds and pruning false hypotheses through floor traversability and multi-view reprojection conflicts.
Demonstrated superior mapping and path planning performance over existing baselines using a real mobile robot on diverse, building-scale datasets totaling more than 2.1 km of traversal.

sections.heading: Why is glass such a headache for robots?
sections.summary: LiDAR misses transparent glass due to its wavelength, transmission, and reflection characteristics, causing collision risks. Prior vision and multimodal reconstruction methods frequently place false obstacles across open paths. This work tackles that trade-off through geometric verification and global management.
sections.details:
Most autonomous mobile robots rely on LiDAR-based SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping). However, transparent glass is notoriously problematic for standard 905 nm small-scale LiDARs. Laser pulses pass straight through glass or reflect specularly in unintended directions, resulting in missing point clouds or ghost points. Consequently, maps are built as if glass walls or automatic doors do not exist, putting the robot at risk of crashing into them.

Techniques using intensity or ultrasonic sensors have been explored, but they require specialized sensors or operate only under narrow angles of incidence. Combining cameras with LiDAR has thus emerged as a promising direction.

Yet reconstructing 3D glass surfaces from images is far from straightforward. Prior work falls into two main approaches, both with noticeable drawbacks:
- Learning-based methods: These estimate glass depth or plane parameters directly from RGB images. But because glass lacks texture and reflects or transmits the surrounding scene, deep networks often misjudge depth.
- Pipeline-based methods: These use 2D detections to fit planes to nearby point clouds, but they often mistake background furniture or foreground occluding edges for glass boundaries, resulting in tilted planes.

Both approaches lead to a fatal navigation error: placing invisible walls right in the middle of walkable corridors or rooms. GlassGuard addresses this dilemma. By assigning each module only the tasks it can reliably perform, verifying candidate planes against depth-free orientation cues from images, and continuously validating them over time in a global map, it achieves high coverage alongside drastically reduced false occupancy.

sections.heading: Previous approaches to glass detection and their limits
sections.summary: Glass perception spans physical-signal methods, 2D image segmentation, and vision-to-3D reconstruction. Existing 3D approaches rely on single-frame predictions without post-verification or subsequent correction.
sections.details:
Prior robotics research on glass perception falls into three broad categories:

- Physical-signal methods: Studies have leveraged laser return intensity, multipath reflections, view-dependent reflection patterns, or supplementary ultrasonic and tactile sensors. However, these depend on specialized sensor setups or work only under specific geometric conditions.
- 2D image-based glass segmentation: In computer vision, polarization cameras, reflection and context modeling, boundary refinement, and foundation models have dramatically improved 2D glass masking accuracy. Even so, 2D masks provide no metric 3D position for navigation maps.
- Vision-to-3D glass reconstruction: Methods like MonoGlass3D predict plane parameters directly from images, while GlassRecon aligns monocular depth priors with RGB-D measurements using RANSAC. Yet these rely on single-frame predictions: once a plane is placed, its orientation and depth are neither verified nor revised later. A single erroneous wall can permanently block the robot's planned path.

GlassGuard overcomes these structural limitations by leveraging robust 2D detection models, depth-free geometric verification, and continuous global hypothesis management.

sections.heading: Two golden rules a navigation map must satisfy
sections.summary: In robot navigation, marking real glass as occupied is just as important as keeping traversable free space unblocked. The authors formalize free-space contamination from misplaced planes as "spill."
sections.details:
For safe, smooth navigation, glass mapping must satisfy two conditions simultaneously: reliably blocking actual glass surfaces, and never obstructing traversable floors or free space.

The paper discretizes the environment into voxels (3D grid cells with side length $\rho$) and formalizes the criteria for an accurate glass map:
1. Voxels containing true glass surfaces must be labeled "occupied" (preventing misses).
2. Voxels in spaces free of physical obstacles must remain "free" and never be marked occupied (preventing misplacement).

The authors designate violations of the second condition—false occupancy in free space—as "spill." As shown in Fig. F1, when a system snaps to occluding background edges, misjudges depth, or gets deceived by specular reflections, it generates tilted phantom planes that cut away the robot's traversable space (false blockages). GlassGuard is designed to minimize spill while thoroughly covering real glass surfaces.

captions.F1: Three common failure modes in plane candidate generation: (a) tilt caused by connecting a frame with a background occluding edge, (b) incorrect depth estimation, and (c) tilt caused by reflections. Red hatched regions represent false blockages (spill) that erroneously obstruct traversable space.

sections.heading: Inside GlassGuard: A three-stage pipeline where each module does what it does best
sections.summary: The system features a robust three-stage design: 2D glass detection via a pruned Slim SAM3, 3D candidate generation from LiDAR features, depth-free monocular geometric orientation checks, and global map consolidation with floor-conflict pruning.
sections.details:
GlassGuard's core design philosophy is simple: assign each module only the tasks it can reliably execute.

### IV-A Overview
The system operates in three main stages (see Fig. F2):
1. Detection and Proposal Generation: A lightweight Slim SAM3 detects 2D masks, and structural pillars are extracted from projected LiDAR points within the mask to form 3D plane hypotheses.
2. Single-Frame Verification: Glass plane tilt is calculated from 2D mask edges without depth information, and candidate planes from LiDAR are ray-cast verified against this horizontal yaw angle.
3. Global Hypothesis Management: Validated planes are not finalized immediately; they are tracked, merged through accumulated LiDAR seeds, and checked against traversable floor evidence and multi-view reprojections over time.

### IV-B Reliable 2D Instance Detection: Slim SAM3
Because all downstream steps depend on 2D masks, high recall is vital. While foundation models like SAM3 are powerful, they consume too much VRAM for onboard mobile robot GPUs. The authors applied Taylor-expansion-based structural pruning and distillation to build "Slim SAM3" specifically for glass. Combined with BF16 and INT8 quantization, this reduced VRAM allocation by roughly two-thirds while preserving strong detection performance.

### IV-C Associate 2D to 3D: Pillar Construction
Raw LiDAR returns off glass are noisy and sparse, so directly fitting planes can introduce severe tilt. Instead, the framework extracts structural features such as mullions and frames within the mask. It identifies "vertical pillars" spanning vertical extents and "horizontal pillars" aligned linearly via 2D PCA, connecting them to form stable metric 3D plane hypotheses.

### IV-D Ray-Cast Orientation Verification
Connecting pillars produces multiple candidate planes, but which one is correct? Here lies the paper's key geometric insight (see Fig. F3).
Two points on a line in an image define an "interpretation plane" passing through the camera center. The intersection line $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}'_1$ between the interpretation planes of two parallel frame edges yields their 3D physical direction vector—without needing depth. For architectural glass where the gravity vector $\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is known (e.g., from an IMU), a single reliable horizontal edge with normal $\mathbf{n}$ uniquely determines the 3D direction as $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{n} \times \hat{\mathbf{g}}$.
The angular error $\Delta\theta$ between this image-derived yaw angle and the LiDAR candidate normal is then evaluated. Because longer glass panels of length $L$ amplify angular errors into larger spills, the acceptance threshold adapts to length: $c \arcsin(2\tau/L)$ (with $\tau=0.5$ m). Passing planes have their horizontal spans clipped by image boundary rays before advancing to the next stage.

### IV-E Global Management
A plane that looks plausible in one frame may prove invalid as the robot moves. GlassGuard maintains three continuous checks in its global manager:
- Global Plane Merging: Overlaps between existing plane tracks and newly observed planes are detected, consolidating and extending them toward whichever side has accumulated more LiDAR seeds.
- Seed and Floor Evidence Maps: A 0.1 m ground grid tracks competing counts for "glass evidence" versus "traversable floor evidence." Any glass plane that intersects voxels confirmed as walkable floor is immediately pruned.
- Multi-View Reprojection Verification: As the robot travels, a correct plane should reproject within the glass mask in new camera views. If its off-mask fraction continuously grows, it is flagged as depth-misestimated and removed.

captions.F3: Principle of depth-free 2D-3D geometric verification. (a) A ray cone is constructed from mask contour edges; (b) the 3D direction (normal) of the glass is recovered from the intersection line of interpretation planes. (c) The angular error $\Delta\theta$ between this visual direction and the LiDAR proposal is checked with a length-adaptive threshold that tightens for longer spans $L$, preventing false path blockages.

sections.heading: 2.1 km of real-robot runs: Fewer misses, without creating phantom walls
sections.summary: Evaluated across nine indoor, outdoor, day, and night environments on a mobile robot, the method achieved 82–85% glass coverage while cutting traversable-space false occupancy voxels by 5 to 17 times compared to baselines.
sections.details:
### V-A Real-World Setup
Experiments used a mecanum-wheel mobile robot equipped with a Livox Mid-360 LiDAR (10 Hz) and a Ricoh Theta panoramic camera (1920×640). GlassGuard ran online on a laptop GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti) at an average of ~0.74 seconds per frame. Evaluation covered six indoor/outdoor environments across nine distinct scenes—including offices, outdoor curtain walls, glass railings, and nighttime glass facades—totaling over 1 hour and 2.1 km of real traversal.

### V-B & V-C Quantitative Analysis
Metrics included "Warning-distance coverage" (how early glass was detected) and "Spill" (the volume of traversable free space erroneously marked occupied).

Compared to leading baselines MonoGlass3D (learning-based) and GlassRecon (pipeline-based), the differences were pronounced:
- Ever Coverage: Under identical pinhole camera fields of view, GlassRecon achieved 44.4% and MonoGlass3D reached 61.0%, whereas the proposed GG-pin achieved 82.1%. With the panoramic camera, GG-360 reached 85.2%.
- False Occupancy (Spill/frame): MonoGlass3D and GlassRecon produced heavy phantom blockages, averaging 290.2 and 85.4 false occupied voxels per frame, respectively. In contrast, GG-pin produced only 16.7 (and GG-360 just 15.3)—a 5- to 17-fold reduction in false obstacles.
- Processing Speed: Under the same pinhole + LiDAR setup, GlassRecon took 3.6 s per frame, whereas GG-pin ran in 0.74 s—nearly 5 times faster.

### V-D Component Ablation
Ablation experiments highlighted the role of each module:
- Disabling the angular verification gate increased co-occurring spill by 75% and boosted cumulative false voxels by 126%, confirming the importance of geometric checks in preventing false blockages.
- Removing multi-view verification improved near-range coverage slightly at the cost of higher overall spill. However, multi-view checks are the only mechanism capable of pruning floating, depth-misestimated planes detached from the floor, serving as a critical safety net.

### V-E Qualitative Analysis
Integrated navigation planner tests (Fig. F4) showed that without glass perception, the robot planned paths straight through closed glass doors. Baselines filled entire corridors with false blue obstacles, resulting in planning failures or excessive detours. GlassGuard cleanly blocked only the true glass boundaries, keeping traversable doors and open hallways clear.

captions.F4: Comparison of glass mapping and local path planning across indoor, outdoor, and day/night scenes. Without glass detection (Glass Blind), dangerous paths cross through glass. Baselines (MonoGlass3D, GlassRecon) clutter corridors with false walls. GlassGuard (GG 360, GG Pinhole) accurately blocks only glass boundaries, preserving safe navigation paths (cyan lines).

sections.heading: Takeaways and future directions
sections.summary: By pairing geometric verification with global evidence management, GlassGuard achieves safe glass mapping for robot navigation. Next steps include handling curved glass and accelerating runtime.
sections.details:
GlassGuard introduces a practical mapping framework for robots navigating environments with transparent architectural glass. By rethinking the problem formulation, verifying plane orientations via depth-free 2D projective geometry, and maintaining global multi-source hypotheses over time, it offers a pragmatic answer to a long-standing dilemma: catching glass obstacles without blocking open walkways.

There is still room for improvement. While ~0.74 s per frame allows online operation, faster rates would improve responsiveness during sharp robot turns. Additionally, the system assumes near-vertical planar glass common in architecture, meaning curved glass or heavily slanted skylights require further extensions. Nevertheless, logging over 2.1 km of trouble-free real-world traversal marks a substantial milestone toward deploying mobile robots safely around glass.

takeaways: Dividing labor—letting learned models handle 2D detection while geometry governs 3D reconstruction and verification—proves far more reliable for deployment than end-to-end 3D learning.
Interpretation planes formed by glass frame lines can uniquely constrain 3D normal directions even when metric depth is entirely unknown, demonstrating the power of classical projective geometry.
Evaluating only obstacle coverage in navigation is hazardous; keeping traversable space free from false blockages (spill) must be co-optimized, or the robot will become trapped.
limitations: Assumes near-vertical planar glass surfaces, so it cannot be directly applied to curved glass or heavily tilted architectural structures.
Average processing time is ~0.74 s per frame (~1.35 Hz), which may cause update lag on robots moving or turning at high speeds.
Relies on 2D image detection; glass surfaces completely lacking frames, mullions, or reflections under flat, uniform lighting may fail to yield initial masks.
